newsitem.title: CHINA: Sleepy China basks in HK handover, urges full unity.
newsitem.headline: Sleepy China basks in HK handover, urges full unity.

text.p: China began its exercise of sovereignty over the returned British colony of Hong Kong on Tuesday with a solemn dawn flag-raising ceremony, a propaganda peal of self-congratulation and calls for full national unification.
Tens of thousands of sleepy invited revellers wrapped up a tightly-organised handover party in Beijing's huge Tiananmen Square with a dawn raising of the nation's five-star flag.

The end of the celebrations included a 76th birthday salute to China's ruling Communist Party, which lost no time in claiming credit for ending more than a century and a half of colonial humiliation at the hands of foreign imperial powers.
"Without the leadership of the Communist Party of China, the motherland cannot become stronger by the day," the official People's Daily said in an editorial.

"Without reform and opening up and without the efforts of new China's third generation of leaders... it would have been impossible for Hong Kong to return," the Xinhua news agency quoted the newspaper as saying.

The People's Daily itself appeared to have become a casualty of the late-night festivities, with no copies immediately available to readers in the capital. Publishers said the newspaper was still being printed late on Tuesday morning.

As Beijing residents rested after the midnight sovereignty switch that ended 156 years of British colonial rule in Hong Kong, state television continued a 72-hour broadcast marathon with playbacks of handover celebrations from around the world.
State radio moved quickly to draw listeners' attention to the next two steps on China's declared road to national unity.
Hong Kong would be an example for the 1999 return to China of the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macau and for reunification with Beijing's island arch-rival Taiwan, it said.

The return of Macau is guaranteed by Sino-Portuguese treaty and by Lisbon's long-standing lack of enthusiasm for retaining the territory, but enticing Taiwan back into the Chinese fold is a far more daunting task for Beijing leaders.
China has considered Taiwan a rebel province since defeated Nationalist government and armies fled to the island after their civil war defeat in 1949.

Beijing offers Taipei reunification under a "One Nation, Two Systems" formula similar to that applied to Hong Kong -- but Taiwan's elected government says China must introduce real democracy before any reunion can be considered.

Analysts say reunification is a key policy goal for China's leadership, which sees boosting patriotic sentiment among the population as a way to bolster communist credentials eroded by nearly two decades of market-style economic reform.

Fears that Taipei was edging toward formal independence prompted Beijing to launch missile tests and war games near the island during its presidential election last year, a move that further chilled ties across the sensitive Taiwan Strait.
People's Daily, the mouthpiece of Beijing's communist leadership, said future unity was assured.
"The Chinese nation will stride ahead with pride into the new century toward the magnificent goal of modernisation," the newspaper said in its editorial.
"The reunification of China and the revitalisation of the Chinese nation will become a glorious fact in the future," it said.
